title: Cable chain stitch
subtitle: A linked chain where a twist of thread connects each loop to the next
excerpt: Cable chain stitch produces a rope-like line of chain loops, each separated by a short bar of thread twisted around the working thread before the next loop is formed. The extra link gives the line more weight and texture than plain chain stitch. It suits borders, stem lines, and any design that needs a slightly heavier mark.
sourceNotes: Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886); Caulfeild & Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882).

glossaryTerms.definition: The length of thread currently being stitched with, running from the fabric to the needle.

content.text: Cable chain stitch looks like a chain with an extra link bolted between each loop. That link is formed by twisting the
working thread
once around the needle before the needle re-enters the fabric. The twist locks on the surface and the next loop grows out of it, giving a heavier, more rope-like line than plain chain stitch.
What you need

items.label: Thread
items.value: Pearl cotton No. 8 or No. 5; stranded cotton 3 to 6 strands for a fuller line

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Medium-weight linen or cotton; the stitch sits proud of the surface so an even weave helps

items.label: Needle
items.value: Crewel needle size 6 or 7; a blunt tapestry needle is harder to manoeuvre for this stitch

items.label: Hoop
items.value: A hoop keeps the fabric taut and makes managing the twist much easier

content.text: Working the stitch
Secure the thread and bring the needle up at point A on your line.
Wrap the working thread once around the needle shaft from left to right (or right to left consistently). Hold that wrap with your thumb so it does not slip off.

Insert the needle into the fabric at point B, a short distance along the line from A. Bring the tip up again at point C, slightly further along, keeping the needle inside the loop of thread that is still around the shaft.

Pull the thread through steadily. The wrap tightens into a short bar on the surface between A and the loop, and the loop closes neatly around point C. Do not pull too tight or the bar will disappear into the fabric.
From C, repeat: wrap the thread around the needle, insert at D close to C, bring up at E, then pull through. Continue along the line, keeping each wrap and loop the same size.
To finish, take the needle down just outside the final loop to hold it flat, then fasten the thread on the back.
Common mistakes

items.symptom: The linking bar vanishes and it looks like plain chain stitch
items.cause: The wrap is not held firmly while inserting the needle, so it slides off before locking.
items.fix: Hold the wrap against the needle shaft with your thumb until the needle is through the fabric and you begin to pull. Use a consistent direction for the wrap every time.

items.symptom: The line puckers or the fabric pulls
items.cause: The needle is re-entering too close to point A, or the thread is pulled too tight after each loop.
items.fix: Leave a small gap between A and B. Use gentle, even tension. Working in a hoop prevents fabric distortion.

content.text: Uses and related stitches
Cable chain stitch is a heavier variation of
chain stitch
and belongs to the same family as
twisted chain stitch
, which uses a different slant to create a knotted effect.
Open chain stitch
takes the opposite approach, widening the loops into a ladder band rather than adding a link between them.
